article.title: AI Is Coming for You, But You Can Fight Back: The Hidden Costs of Artificial Intelligence
article.author: Frieda Afary
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Artificial intelligence is being sold to the public as the next great technological revolution, promising unprecedented productivity, scientific breakthroughs, and solutions to some of humanity's most difficult problems. But who benefits from this transformation, who pays its costs, and who gets to decide how the technology is deployed? Those questions drove a panel titled “AI Is Coming for You, But You Can Fight Back” at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. Moderated by Iranian American writer, librarian, and socialist feminist Frieda Afary, the discussion featured environmental scientist Pablo Ortiz Partida of the Union of Concerned Scientists, education researcher Nick Rabb, and environmental journalist Bill Kelly. Together, they challenged the narrative that artificial intelligence represents inevitable progress, arguing instead that its rapid expansion reflects decisions made by powerful corporations and institutions, often without meaningful public participation. AI Is Coming For You (1:08:07) The Environmental Costs Hidden Behind the Cloud Pablo Ortiz Partida began by dismantling one of the technology industry's central illusions: that the digital world exists somewhere apart from the physical environment. The cloud, he explained, consists of enormous buildings filled with computers requiring electricity, cooling systems, water, and extensive infrastructure. The new generation of hyperscale data centers being constructed for artificial intelligence represents something fundamentally different from conventional computing facilities. Some proposed complexes encompass hundreds or thousands of acres and require electricity comparable to that consumed by substantial population centers. Ortiz Partida described how these facilities can strain water supplies, increase electricity demand, produce air pollution through diesel backup generators, and subject neighboring communities to constant industrial noise. He also discussed the trade-offs involved in cooling systems. Technologies that reduce electricity consumption may require more water, while those conserving water may consume additional energy. Crucially, he emphasized that most of a data center's water footprint can occur indirectly through electricity generation rather than at the facility itself. That means regulations addressing only water consumed on-site may overlook much of the environmental burden. The consequences are not distributed equally. Communities living near data centers may experience rising energy costs, noise, pollution, and additional heat while receiving relatively few of the promised economic benefits. Ortiz Partida distinguished between targeted applications of machine learning that can assist climate research and medicine and the far more resource-intensive generative AI systems driving much of today's infrastructure expansion. His argument was not that every application of artificial intelligence is harmful, but that society must evaluate its benefits against its environmental and social costs. Related: AI, Surveillance and War: Who Is Emerging Technology Really Serving? Is AI Undermining Education and Critical Thinking? Nick Rabb, a postdoctoral researcher studying AI and education, offered an equally troubling assessment of the technology's impact on classrooms. Rabb examined the California State University system's multimillion-dollar agreement with OpenAI to provide ChatGPT access across its campuses. The arrangement was promoted as a way to provide personalized tutoring, improve educational opportunities, and help instructors manage their workloads. But Rabb questioned whether the evidence justified those promises. After reviewing research on large language models in educational settings, he concluded that their use frequently undermines learning, especially when students depend on them to perform intellectual tasks they need to master themselves. Students who already possess strong study habits and critical-thinking abilities may benefit in limited circumstances, he explained. Those who lack such foundations may become increasingly dependent on technology that performs their thinking for them. Rather than closing educational inequalities, widespread AI adoption could therefore deepen them. Rabb also warned that language models reproduce biases embedded in their training material and can reinforce users' existing assumptions. Students must learn to evaluate evidence, recognize flawed arguments, and challenge ideological assumptions—not simply accept plausible-sounding answers generated by commercial systems. His criticism extended beyond classroom performance to the governance of public universities. Rabb described how faculty committees and task forces had examined the implications of AI, yet major institutional decisions could still be imposed from above. For him, this illustrated a broader democratic problem: corporations and university administrators increasingly determine how education is organized, while educators and students have limited power over those decisions. AI's Expanding Ecological Footprint Environmental journalist Bill Kelly widened the discussion beyond data centers to the global supply chains required to build them. Kelly, author of Smogtown: The Lung-Burning History of Los Angeles and The People's Republic of Chemicals , argued that the environmental costs of artificial intelligence begin long before a server is switched on. The metals needed for computer equipment are extracted from mines, frequently in countries in the Global South where environmental protections and labor standards may be weak. Mining can destroy landscapes, contaminate water supplies, and expose nearby communities to hazardous pollution. Those materials must then be transported, refined, manufactured into components, and shipped again before reaching data centers. Each stage requires energy and generates additional environmental damage. Kelly also emphasized the short useful lives of advanced computing equipment. Servers containing substantial quantities of valuable metals may be replaced after only a few years, contributing to an already enormous global electronic-waste problem. He warned that the coming expansion of robotics could multiply these pressures. For Kelly, the underlying issue is an economic system dependent on continuous growth, even as humanity approaches or exceeds critical ecological limits. He urged governments to distinguish socially beneficial uses of AI from applications designed primarily to maximize profits, eliminate jobs, expand surveillance, or intensify consumption. Related: AI "Friends" Are a Big Joke—But You Shouldn't Laugh Workers, Surveillance, and the Question of Power The discussion repeatedly returned to the consequences of artificial intelligence for working people. Kelly pointed to warehouse surveillance systems capable of monitoring employees' movements and hospital staffing technologies that can prioritize cost reduction over patient care. He also raised concerns about artificial intelligence replacing performers and other entertainment workers, potentially depriving them of employment and benefits. The panel connected these developments to the expansion of surveillance technologies and the growing power of corporations to control workplaces, public institutions, and information. In the audience discussion, participants drew comparisons with the nineteenth-century Luddites, whose resistance to industrial machinery was rooted in conflicts over labor, ownership, and economic power. The question was not simply whether new machines could perform human tasks, but whether technological development would enhance human freedom or strengthen existing systems of exploitation. Fighting Back Means Reclaiming Democratic Control Despite their criticisms, the panelists did not suggest that resistance was futile. Rabb described students who deliberately avoid using language models because they recognize the importance of developing their own intellectual abilities. Participants emphasized the need for technological, environmental, and economic literacy—particularly the ability to distinguish genuine scientific advances from exaggerated corporate promises. Kelly called for enforceable environmental standards, responsible supply chains, longer equipment lifespans, and restrictions on socially destructive applications of artificial intelligence. The larger challenge, however, was political. The panel suggested that decisions about technologies affecting education, employment, public health, civil liberties, and the environment cannot remain exclusively in the hands of corporate executives and institutional administrators. The question is not whether artificial intelligence will continue developing. It is whether democratic societies can assert control over how that development proceeds, whose interests it serves, and what costs humanity is willing to bear. At the Left Coast Forum, the message was that fighting back begins by rejecting technological inevitability and insisting that people—not corporations or algorithms—determine the future.
